Sandwich Variances with a Leverage Correction

Source: R/sandwich_hc23.R
hc2_sandwich.Rd

Select the meat of the frequentist variance \(V = V_b B V_b\) with the scores of the observations rescaled by their leverage: hc2_sandwich() and hc3_sandwich(), which with a cluster are the cluster-robust estimators CR2 and CR3, and hc4_sandwich(). Pass the object as the sandwich argument of frequentist_vcov().

Usage

hc2_sandwich(
  cluster = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  reference = c("t", "normal"),
  weights = c("frequency", "sampling")
)

hc3_sandwich(cluster = NULL, data = NULL, weights = c("frequency", "sampling"))

hc4_sandwich(weights = c("frequency", "sampling"))

Arguments

cluster

NULL (the default) or a one-sided formula with a single variable of the data, such as ~ id.

data

NULL (the default) or the data frame that holds the cluster variable, with one row for each observation of the fit.

reference

For hc2_sandwich() with a cluster: "t" (the default) or "normal", the reference distribution of the Wald intervals and tests.

weights

"frequency" (the default) or "sampling": whether the prior weights of the fit are frequencies or sampling weights, as at hc0_sandwich().

Value

A SandwichMethod object with the properties type ("HC2", "HC3" or "HC4"), cluster, data, reference and weights.

Details

Let \(s_i\) be the vector of the derivatives of the log-likelihood of observation \(i\) in the \(d\) predictors of the model, \(Z_i\) the \(d \times P\) matrix that places the design rows of the observation in the stacked coefficients, \(W_i\) the \(d \times d\) information of the observation, and \(H_{ii}\) its leverage block, as defined at statmod_leverage(). The score of the observation is \(u_i = Z_i' s_i\). Each estimator replaces \(s_i\) by $$s_i^* = W_i^{1/2}\, (I - H_{ii})^{-p}\, W_i^{-1/2}\, s_i,$$ and then forms \(B = \sum_i u_i^* u_i^{*\prime}\) with \(u_i^* = Z_i' s_i^*\). The estimators differ in the exponent \(p\):

  • HC2 (hc2_sandwich()): \(p = 1/2\), as in MacKinnon and White (1985);

  • HC3 (hc3_sandwich()): \(p = 1\), as in MacKinnon and White (1985);

  • HC4 (hc4_sandwich()): one exponent for each equation \(a\), \(\delta_{ia} = \min\{4, h_{i,aa}/\bar h_a\}\), where \(h_{i,aa}\) is the diagonal element of \(H_{ii}\) for that equation and \(\bar h_a\) its mean over the observations, as in Cribari-Neto (2004) for each equation. The power \((I - H_{ii})^{-p}\) is replaced by $$F_i = \exp\big(-\tfrac12\, D_i \log(I - H_{ii})\, D_i\big), \qquad D_i = \mathrm{diag}(\delta_{i1}^{1/2}, \ldots, \delta_{id}^{1/2}),$$ which is \(\mathrm{diag}\{(1 - h_{i,aa})^{-\delta_{ia}/2}\}\) when \(H_{ii}\) is diagonal and \((I - H_{ii})^{-\delta_i/2}\) when the exponents of the equations are equal.

The matrix power is taken on the eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix \(H_{ii}\). When a model has one equation, \(W_i\) is a scalar and \(s_i^* = s_i (1 - h_i)^{-p}\), the textbook estimators; for a Gaussian linear model with a constant scale they equal the estimators built from stats::hatvalues(). An eigenvalue of \(H_{ii}\) equal to one (a direction that the fit reproduces exactly) is given the factor zero, which is the pseudo-inverse, and a warning reports it; under HC4 the block of such an observation is corrected by the power with the mean of its exponents.

With cluster = ~ id, the observations of a cluster \(g\) are corrected together: \(s_g^* = W_g^{1/2}\,(I - H_{gg})^{-p}\,W_g^{-1/2}\,s_g\), where \(s_g\) stacks the vectors \(s_i\) of its observations, \(W_g\) is block diagonal and \(H_{gg}\) is the diagonal block of the hat matrix for the cluster, of dimension equal to the number of observations in the cluster times \(d\). The exponent \(1/2\) is CR2 (Bell and McCaffrey, 2002; Pustejovsky and Tipton, 2018) and the exponent \(1\) is CR3. A cluster with one observation each reduces them to HC2 and HC3. hc4_sandwich() has no cluster argument, since no version of HC4 for clusters is established. The estimators apply no degrees-of-freedom factor, so that hc2_sandwich() and hc3_sandwich() coincide with hc0_sandwich() when the leverage is zero.

The correction is the exact bias removal for the linearized fit when the working model is the model itself (the observations independent, with variance \(W_i^{-1}\) for their scores), and it uses the information selected by the information argument of frequentist_vcov() when it is given, for the roots \(W_i^{1/2}\) as well as for the inverse \(K^{-1}\). When that argument is NULL, the leverage is computed on the expected information, whatever information the bread \(V_b\) resolves for the family. With the observed information, an observation whose matrix \(W_i\) is indefinite contributes the positive part, with the pseudo-inverse root (statmod_leverage() returns how many observations that concerns). With penalties the leverage is that of the penalized fit, and the sum of the traces is the effective degrees of freedom computed on the information of the leverage, which equals the degrees of freedom of the fit only when the fit reads the same information (statmod_leverage() gives the conditions). Prior weights, random effects, aliased coordinates and the models that are rejected are treated as at hc0_sandwich(). Prior weights enter the leverage through \(W_i\); without a cluster the leverage of one of the \(w_i\) copies of a row is \(1/w_i\) times that of the row, which is what the estimator uses, and with a cluster the copies of a row are corrected within the cluster. With weights = "sampling" and no cluster the leverage is that of the row, not divided by \(w_i\), and the mean leverage of each equation in HC4 is the mean over the rows with positive weight.

Few clusters. With CR2 and reference = "t" (the default), confint.StatmodFit() and the Wald rows of summary.StatmodFit() and statmod_test() use a \(t\) distribution whose degrees of freedom are computed for each coefficient by the Satterthwaite approximation of Pustejovsky and Tipton (2018). For a coefficient \(c'\beta\), with \(t_g = (I - H_{gg})^{-1/2} W_g^{1/2} Z_g V_b c\), the variance estimate is \(\sum_g (t_g' \hat r_g)^2\) in the standardized scores \(\hat r = W^{-1/2}\hat s\). If the true standardized scores \(r\) had identity covariance, then \(\hat r = (I - H) r\) and the estimate is a quadratic form of \(r\) whose degrees of freedom are \((\sum_g q_g'q_g)^2 / \sum_{g,h} (q_g'q_h)^2\), where \(q_g\) is the vector \((I - H)\, t_g\) with \(t_g\) placed in the rows of cluster \(g\). reference = "normal" keeps the normal distribution. The other sandwich types always use the normal distribution.

References

MacKinnon, J. G. and White, H. (1985). Some heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimators with improved finite sample properties. Journal of Econometrics, 29(3), 305–325.

Bell, R. M. and McCaffrey, D. F. (2002). Bias reduction in standard errors for linear regression with multi-stage samples. Survey Methodology, 28(2), 169–181.

Cribari-Neto, F. (2004). Asymptotic inference under heteroskedasticity of unknown form. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 45(2), 215–233.

Pustejovsky, J. E. and Tipton, E. (2018). Small-sample methods for cluster-robust variance estimation and hypothesis testing in fixed effects models. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 36(4), 672–683.

See also

hc0_sandwich(), statmod_leverage(), frequentist_vcov().

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(150), id = rep(1:30, each = 5))
dd$y <- 1 + 2 * dd$x + rnorm(150, sd = 0.2 + dd$x)
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, vcov_type = frequentist_vcov(
  sandwich = hc3_sandwich()), param = "mu")))
#> mu:(Intercept)           mu:x 
#>     0.09543413     0.24453148 
vcov(fit, vcov_type = frequentist_vcov(
  sandwich = hc2_sandwich(cluster = ~ id)), param = "mu")
#>                mu:(Intercept)        mu:x
#> mu:(Intercept)     0.01074648 -0.02488978
#> mu:x              -0.02488978  0.07485765
